name: Clarkson University

profile.address: Old Main, Main Street, Village of Potsdam, Town of Potsdam, Saint Lawrence County, New York, 13676
profile.reading:
Old Main is one of the oldest and most architecturally distinctive buildings on Clarkson University's campus in the village of Potsdam, in New York's North Country. It was built using red sandstone quarried along the Raquette River from operations run by the university's founder, Thomas S. Clarkson. That same stone was used for accent work on Canada's Parliament buildings in Ottawa and for All Saints Cathedral in Albany. It gives Old Main, along with other early campus structures such as Woodstock Lodge, a distinctive look tied directly to the region's industrial and geological history rather than to a generic institutional style.

Clarkson University itself is a private research university best known for engineering, business, and health sciences programs, with an enrollment concentrated in STEM fields and a campus culture built around hands on, applied research. The university's public facing computing resources are concentrated in newer or renovated spaces, including the largely student run Applied CS Labs, which house the Clarkson Open Source Institute, an Internet Teaching Lab, and a Virtual Reality Lab, plus the Clarkson Ignite makerspaces used for prototyping and fabrication. The Open Source Institute in particular operates a mirror server that provides public downloads for open source projects such as Blender and Ubuntu, a role that requires real server and network infrastructure but is described by the university in terms of the service it provides rather than the room or building housing the hardware.

Old Main's own current occupants are not detailed in the university's public facing materials in a way that identifies it specifically as a data center or server facility. Given its age and the way Clarkson documents its computing spaces elsewhere on campus, it is far more likely that any IT infrastructure in or near Old Main serves the ordinary operational needs of the university, administrative systems, network equipment closets, or research computing tied to specific departments, rather than functioning as the university's primary enterprise data center. Small private universities of Clarkson's size typically run modest, in house computing operations sized to campus enrollment rather than large scale facilities, and they rarely publish equipment inventories, power draw, or square footage for those spaces the way commercial data center operators do, since the audience for that information is internal IT staff rather than the public or prospective tenants.

reading:
Clarkson University is a private technological university in Potsdam, in the North Country of New York, and it is in this registry for an unusual reason. It sells colocation. Its service, branded colo at Old Main, offers enterprise grade rack space to organisations outside the university, which makes it a genuine if very small commercial operator rather than a campus machine room that a mapping project mistook for one.

The registry's single record is worth reading carefully. It is an OpenStreetMap building polygon covering the whole of Old Main, tagged at once as a university, as an education building and as a data centre, with a building use of data centre, drawn from United States Geological Survey place name data and referenced back to the colocation service's own web address. Old Main is the university's original building, on Main Street in the village of Potsdam, roughly three quarters of a mile from the main campus at 8 Clarkson Avenue. The colocation suite occupies part of that building. The polygon is the building, so a registry that treats the polygon as the facility records a whole multi purpose university building as a data centre, and any floor area derived from it would be wrong by a wide margin.

What Clarkson publishes about the facility is infrastructure description rather than capacity. It cites three layers of card access control, dry agent fire suppression, monitoring around the clock, dual uninterruptible power supply feeds, N plus one generator capacity, full automatic transfer switching tested weekly, redundant cooling with continuous environmental monitoring, blended high speed bandwidth from multiple providers, dedicated circuits available from several carriers, and physically diverse paths out of the region, which is a real concern in the St Lawrence valley. Space is sold by the rack unit, the half height cabinet or the full height cabinet, and authorised customers get unescorted access at any hour. Enquiries route to the university's own information technology helpdesk, so the service is run by Clarkson's IT organisation rather than by a separate company.

What it does not publish is equally clear. There is no square footage for the data hall, no critical IT load, no utility service size, no generator rating in kilowatts and no launch year for the service. The registry therefore carries no capacity for this site, and that is the correct state rather than a gap to be filled by estimate.

Separately, Clarkson researchers have won National Science Foundation awards for high performance computing clusters, so the university also runs research computing for its own account. That internal capability and the customer facing colocation service are different things and should not be added together.
